title: The lamp of the eye (Luke 11:14–36)
hookLine: take heed that the light in you is not darkness

cards: This part of Luke is noisy. Jesus heals a man who couldn't speak, and some in the crowd say he does it by the power of the prince of demons. He answers that a house divided against itself falls.

A woman shouts a blessing on his mother. Others demand a sign from heaven. And in the middle of all that heat, he stops and talks about something quiet: a lamp in a room, and the light that comes in through your eyes.

teach.b: First, the lamp. Nobody lights one and hides it under a bushel; you set it on a stand so whoever walks in can see.

Then, in the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness."
Single sounds odd to us. The Greek word, haplous, means simple, whole, undivided: an eye that sees clearly because it isn't split between ten things.
And in Jesus' world, a good eye and an evil eye were also ways of talking about money and people.

teach.h: A GOOD EYE IS A GENEROUS EYE.
teach.b: A generous person had a good eye; a stingy, envious one had an evil eye. Proverbs says: "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor."
Paul later uses a word from the same family as haplous for generosity. So the saying is about more than eyesight. How you look at people fills you up.
Look at the world with envy or suspicion, and the darkness gets inside. Look with a clear, generous eye, and you fill with light.
Then a short, sharp warning: "Take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness."

teach.h: THE LIGHT OF THE BODY IS THE EYE.
teach.b: You can think you're seeing clearly and be wrong. In a chapter full of people who looked straight at a healing and saw the devil, that line lands hard. The crowd wanted a sign from the sky.
He points them back to their own eyes.

how: Some Christians practice a slow, attentive looking as prayer, with icons in Orthodox churches, with art and nature in many retreat traditions, and with the Ignatian habit of noticing where God was present in the day.

o: alone, with no one else around

games.q: what's inside Luke 11:14–36 — tap the pairs.
p: set on a stand, not under a bushel

s: in Jesus' world, a good eye could mean a generous person
a good eye was generous, an evil eye stingy and envious. Proverbs: "he that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed."
the Greek haplous means simple, whole, undivided.
Jesus gives the crowd the sign from heaven they demand
he points them to the sign of Jonah and to the light they already have.

games.q: a crowd has just watched a man healed. some say it's the devil's work; others demand a sign from heaven. what does Jesus point them to?
o: their own eyes, and the light already in them.
games.why: he talks about a lamp and says the light of the body is the eye: "take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness."

practice: Find one thing in front of you or out of a window, a tree, a face in a photo, the light on a wall, a cup, and let your eyes rest on it alone, bringing them back whenever your attention splits.

Look at it generously, the way you'd look at something you love, without judging it or wanting anything from it. If you pray, give thanks for what you see; if not, notice what happens inside you as you look.

wordCard.voice: Haplous, Greek for single, simple, whole: Jesus says the eye is the body's light, and a clear, generous eye like that fills you with light, while an envious one lets the darkness in.

orig.note: Greek: single, simple, whole. the King James Bible says single; a related word means generosity.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the light in. A clear eye is a generous one. Day five hundred forty-five, done.
